title: Yes Bank Faces Rs 5,217 Crore Pro Forma Hit After Supreme Court AT-1 Ruling
excerpt: Yes Bank says recognising the Supreme Court verdict that quashed its Rs 8,415 crore AT-1 bond write-off would have turned its September-quarter profit into a Rs 5,217 crore loss and cut its CET-1 ratio to 11.4%. Japan's SMBC, which now owns 24.9%, bought in while the case was pending.
body:
• Yes Bank reported a September-quarter net profit of Rs 1,080 crore, up 65% year on year — but says the figure would have been a net loss of Rs 5,217 crore if it had recognised the Supreme Court's AT-1 judgment.
  • The court upheld the quashing of the March 2020 write-off of Rs 8,415 crore of additional tier-1 bonds, imposed during the bank's RBI-led reconstruction.
  • On the bank's pro forma numbers, its CET-1 capital ratio would fall to 11.4% from the reported 13.7%, and return on assets would swing to negative 4.3% from positive 0.9%.
  • For shareholders: the bank has recognised no impact yet and is assessing legal and accounting options, so the size and timing of any capital raise remain open.

Yes Bank would have reported a net loss of Rs 5,217 crore in the September quarter had it recognised the impact of the Supreme Court verdict overturning the write-off of its additional tier-1 (AT-1) bonds worth Rs 8,415 crore, the bank said in its second-quarter investor presentation filed with the stock exchanges.

Instead, the private-sector lender reported a net profit of Rs 1,080 crore for July-September, up 65% year on year. Net interest income rose 22.7% to Rs 2,822 crore, operating profit rose 29.4% to Rs 1,678 crore, and gross non-performing assets improved to 1.2% from 1.6% a year earlier, according to the presentation reported by TradingView News.

What the Court Decided

The Supreme Court held the write-off of the AT-1 bonds to be illegal and arbitrary, upholding the Bombay High Court's 2023 decision. The bonds were written off in March 2020 by the administrator appointed under Yes Bank's reconstruction scheme, while equity holders were subjected only to a three-year lock-in on 75% of their shares — an asymmetry bondholders challenged, arguing the bonds were mis-sold and could not be written off after the final scheme was gazetted.

"The Supreme Court has held the write-off of AT-1 bonds by the Administrator of Yes Bank to be illegal and arbitrary on the ground of it being against the Final Reconstruction Scheme gazetted by the Union of India."

— Srijan Sinha, partner at Edictum Law & Co., representing AT-1 bondholders, via The Hindu BusinessLine

Shares of Yes Bank fell 13% on the day of the ruling, The Hindu BusinessLine reported, and are down more than 20% in two weeks, according to Mint.

The SMBC Question

Japan's Sumitomo Mitsui Banking Corporation agreed to acquire a 20% stake in Yes Bank in May 2025 and raised it by a further 4.99% in August 2025, taking its holding to about 24.9% and making it the bank's largest shareholder. The AT-1 litigation was pending and publicly disclosed throughout that period — rating agencies had flagged before the verdict that an adverse ruling could cut CET-1 by roughly 230-250 basis points. Moneycontrol reported, citing sources, that SMBC was aware of the AT-1 litigation risk ahead of the deal. Whether the transaction documents protect SMBC from pre-investment liabilities has not been disclosed; one senior advocate quoted by CNBC-TV18 argued that if the new investor is protected, the burden falls on existing shareholders, and the bank may need to raise capital or launch a rights issue.

What Happens Next

Yes Bank said the pro forma estimates are subject to revision based on consequential actions, further legal assessment and the final accounting and regulatory treatment, and that it is evaluating options to strengthen its capital buffers. No impact has been recognised in the reported results. For investors, the open variables are the remedy the court process produces, whether bondholders are reinstated at par with unpaid coupons, and how much fresh capital the bank raises — and at what price.
